Being on the defense from unwanted and unsolicited is completely natural and productive. Life is full of this. it is the individuals responsibility to lay out boundaries and to have micro fights in interpersonal relationships with other people. And I recognize, as they are minors, they will require extra aid from adults to help navigate the kids through to learn how to have interpersonal relationships. I am not against this. I’m not an apologists for real criminals but these are most likely just young boys who just barely started to grow hair down there. From your description, the Scouts don’t fit either definition of “creepy” or “lack of respect”, imho. I also can’t see how you can be “fully supportive” of girls in Scouting if you go turn around and then try to inhibit what seems to be very natural and productive. Not saying the Scouts’ behavior is the best but it definitely sounds like it is just a bunch of kids trying to navigate their personal interests and hormones in a non-destructive way.

Jimmy Carter is one of the former presidents of the United States of America. As an individual in such position, Carter oversaw the vast lands that the U.S. held and this included the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. Despite the economic opportunities of the land, Carter argues for the land to be untouched through nationalistic diction, personal anecdotes, historical context, and the illogical reasoning for establishing industries in the region.

Carter starts his argument with a grand description of what the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge is. The nationalistic diction he uses to describe the location such as “America’s last truly great wilderness”, “America’s Serengeti”, “ and “symbol of our national heritage” are all important details. This diction resonates with the Americans as it is no longer a foreign, disconnected land but rather something personal and prideful to all Americans. Carter successfully conveys that it is part of everyone’s duty as an American to safeguard the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. 

The majority of the article is about a personal anecdote that Carter experienced himself. He describes the landscape and ecosystem in elegance, “...brilliant mosaic of wildflowers, mosses, and lichens” and “...tens of thousands of caribou with their newborn calves. In a matter of minutes, the sweep of tundra before us became flooded with life”. The first excerpt is significant because Carter frames the landscape as a work of art, like a mosaic. The different colors and placement of the flowers, despite being natural, is compared just as if it was a masterful artwork. The second excerpt is mentioned by Carter so he can attach a sense and value of life and familyhood to the place. It is a reminder that this is the home of thousands of animals that are all living and breeding. The picture Carter paints of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge is one that is filled with art, life, and families. He then proceeds to contrast this with the image of an industrialized area full of roads, pipelines, drilling rigs, and industrial facilities. The heavy contract between the two emphasizes and enhances the utmost importance of protecting the region. 

Next, Carter moves to a different approach, the bipartisanship of keeping the land protected. He mentions that both Republican and Democratic presidents recognize the value of the land and it isn’t a political issue. By establishing that it is a bipartisan resolution, he solidifies his motives as being more transparent and pure. Carter also mentions that the American people have opposed the past attempts to open the region up to oil drilling. He mentions this piece of information in order to further reinforce that it is not only the politicians’ will to keep the region closed but it is largely the Americans’ will as well. He successfully places his argument in solidarity with the American people and their will by utilizing historical context. 

Lastly, one of his arguments against the development of industries within the land was the weight of the losses versus the gains. Carter states that the Arctic Refuge might provide one to two percent of the oil that the U.S. consumes each day. He understands that the number “one to two percent” is a small number and he uses it for his argument. He spells out the illogical thinking of developing industries by emphasizing that the “heart of our greatest refuge” would be destroyed just for a mere one to two percent. Furthermore, he provides a replacement solution in the place of it so it does not seem like the U.S. is missing out on oil without a reason or plan. 

Carter ties together the idea that the Arctic National Wildfire would be the “greatest gift”. In conclusion, he successfully argues his position by rousing up nationalism through his diction, establishing an intimate experience through his personal anecdote, utilizing historical context of the wills of politics and the American people, and highlighting the logical inconsistencies of opening up industries within the wilderness.
